Tech Report: Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.
  • Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.
  • The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” remarked the organization. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”.

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”.

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino claims that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an crucial part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”.

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”.

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”.

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos rolled out earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

How Pets at Home's vibrant fresh family solves the biggest challenge of designing sub-brands

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Designing a sub-brand is hard enough.
  • For Pets, HOW+HOW tackled the brief by creating a cohesive brand ecosystem that both unites and distinguishes the brands.
  • Pets is best known for its Pets at Home retail stores, of which there are around 450 in the UK, but it also has around 400 veterinary practices, 300 grooming salons, and it's expanded into into insurance, charity initiatives and a children’s club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Designing a sub-brand is hard enough. Designing three at once, each serving a different audience, takes the challenge to another level.

For Pets, HOW+HOW tackled the brief by creating a cohesive brand ecosystem that both unites and distinguishes the brands. Each member of the family stands on its own while clearly remaining part of the larger story. The agency's founder, CEO and creative director Cath How tells us how they approached the task.

Pets is best known for its Pets at Home retail stores, of which there are around 450 in the UK, but it also has around 400 veterinary practices, 300 grooming salons, and it's expanded into into insurance, charity initiatives and a children’s club. HOW+HOW had the task of revamping the brand identities for the Pets Insurance, Pets Foundation and Pet Pals sub brands.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest challenges was going to be avoiding the trap that many brand ecosystems fall into: consistency becoming sameness. The objective was to create a characterful and flexible system of brands that share common DNA but don't feel like copies. Each one would need specific creative treatments tailored to their audience.

"We treated Pets as a brand family rather than one masterbrand repeated three times," Cat claims. "Each sub-brand needed a clear role, personality and reason to exist, while still feeling unmistakably part of Pets. The test was whether each could stand confidently on its own, but still lead people back to the same place.

"Consistency had to come from shared principles rather than identical outputs. We created a flexible system with common connective cues, but gave each sub-brand room to express its own tone and character. The aim was to make the family feel related, not repetitive.".

In a recent development, three distinct personalities run from the sub-brands' naming to their visual and verbal identities, illustration, web design and campaign developments. Pets Insurance (above) needed a bold, energetic positioning to stand out in a crowded category, but it also needed to be clear, reassuring and to strike an empathetic verbal tone given that it's a brand that's put to the test during difficult moments for its customers.

Meanwhile, Pet Pals, the kids' club, becomes a fully realised vibrant illustrated universe, populated by a cast of animal characters that wouldn't look out of place in a TV animation (see below). This creates a host of storytelling opportunities and extends into merchandising and wider brand experiences, taking the opportunity to deepen emotional engagement with audiences already invested in their pets.

"Pets already has a naturally warm, emotional relationship with its audiences, so there was a real opportunity to build a world people could feel part of," Cat notes. "Characters give each part of the family a memorable personality, while merchandising makes the brand tangible and more participatory. It needed to feel like more than a visual identity. A world with room to grow.".

Finally, Pets Foundation gets a more emotionally driven treatment, focused on helping both animals and people. Motion graphic pieces, which Cat calls ‘zoomies’, inject added dynamism to its brand.

According to recent reports, underpinning all of the creative decisions was a close examination of customer behaviour. Rather than organising the architecture around internal business structures, How+How focused on how pet owners actually move through the ecosystem.

"People don't experience petcare in neat internal categories," Cat points out. "They move between buying products, seeking advice, booking a vet appointment, arranging insurance and looking for support. The ecosystem needed to reflect those real-life journeys, making the different services feel connected and easy to navigate.".

An emphasis on growth and long-term flexibility is evident across the whole system, which was designed to be capable of accommodating future expansion while maintaining recognisability.

Industry observers note that but how do you measure the success of a project like this? Cath believes that involves more than visual recognition alone.

Industry observers note that "Recognition is only the starting point. We would also look at whether people understand the role of each sub-brand, can move easily between different services, and feel a stronger sense of connection with Pets as a whole. Engagement, audience sentiment, cross-brand consideration and commercial performance will all be important measures over time.".

In an increasingly fragmented brand landscape, the Pets project offers a reminder that successful brand architecture isn't simply about visual consistency. It's about creating systems that help audiences understand relationships between products and services while giving each expression enough personality to earn attention in its own right.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.
  • It has been revealed that keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal.
  • European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

It has been revealed that keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins notes about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal challenges and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

In a recent development, two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

Recent findings suggest that “She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins states this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins states you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

It has been revealed that coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins notes change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hauser & Wirth now represents Ser Serpas, a fast-rising artist known for her poetically minded installations and haunting paintings.
  • She will have her first solo show with Hauser & Wirth at its Paris space in January.
  • According to recent reports, born and raised in Los Angeles’s Boyle Heights neighborhood, Serpas is an itinerant artist who is primarily based in Paris but also “regularly moves between such cities as New York, Los Angeles, Geneva, and Tbilisi,” according to a release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hauser & Wirth now represents Ser Serpas, a fast-rising artist known for her poetically minded installations and haunting paintings. Hauser & Wirth will represent the artist in collaboration with her longtime gallery LC Queisser, which has spaces in Tbilisi, Georgia, and Cologne, Germany.

She will have her first solo show with Hauser & Wirth at its Paris space in January. For that exhibition, Serpas will show a new series of paintings, as well as debut a multimedia installation. Born in 1995, she is one of the youngest artists to be represented by Hauser & Wirth, and one of a handful Latinx artists to show with the gallery, which added to its roster rafa esparza earlier this month. Related Articles Hauser & Wirth Now Represents rafa esparza, Maker of Adobe Sculptures and Paintings That Center Community Frieze London Brings 400-Year-Old Paintings and Collectors in Their 20s.

According to recent reports, born and raised in Los Angeles’s Boyle Heights neighborhood, Serpas is an itinerant artist who is primarily based in Paris but also “regularly moves between such cities as New York, Los Angeles, Geneva, and Tbilisi,” according to a release. Her practice is equally disparate, spanning various mediums from sculpture and painting to video and photography to poetry and performance.

Serpas is best known for her sculptures and installations in which she brings together the detritus of everyday life, giving the found objects that comprise them new life and meaning. She gathers the items from the streets where she is living or in residency. “I’m building a palette every time I go into a new city,” she has mentioned of her process. In a 2023 New York Times profile, she described “Parisian trash [as] sturdy.”.

Recent findings suggest that to make her works, Serpas usually works alone, constructing the pieces in situ. She often tells the venues she will show at, “OK, you have to give me the key and there’s going to be a lot of things in the recycling and I might have some friends over, but you just have to trust me and you’ll get a show. But on my terms.”.

Often, these installations make poignant, if oblique, references to today’s most pressing issues. An installation for the 2024 Whitney Biennial, for example, featured a tattered US flag laying on “a disused piece of a sectional relegated to the corner—which is perhaps where the Stars and Stripes belongs during these depressing times,” as ARTnews’s Alex Greenberger wrote in his review. The 2025 work tube of brief cadavers made sadder still, which featured on ARTnews’s list of “The Defining Artworks of 2025,” combined elements that recalled the ongoing migrant crisis.

Serpas also has an active painting practice, which often features ambiguous figures, initially depicting those of her lovers and people before and after surgery. Perhaps in a nod to her interest in horror and the uncanny, she presses two wet canvases together to create a ghost image. Since 2023, Serpas has used AI to generate the bodies that animate and distort her paintings.

“For the first time, I’m showing paintings in a pretty traditional way, and I know that’s going to ask a lot from people who are familiar with my sculptural practice,” Serpas told the Art Newspaper in 2025, of her show at Kunsthalle Basel that summer. “The sculptures are difficult to contend with for many collectors and institutions, and I do wish more people had them in their homes. Some people do, but not as many as the paintings, drawings or even some of the sound-based multimedia pieces I’ve made.”.

Over the past decade, Serpas has become one of her generation’s most closely watched and in-demand artists. She has had institutional solo exhibitions at Kölnischer Kunstverein in Cologne (through December 13), Contemporary Art Gallery in Vancouver (2026), Kunsthalle Basel (2025), the Swiss Institute in New York (2023), and the Museum Ludwig in Cologne (2023). In addition to the 2024 Whitney Biennial, Serpas has also been included in “Flow States: La Trienal 2024” at El Museo del Barrio, “The Gatherers” (2025) at MoMA PS1, and the 2020 Made in L.A. biennial at the Hammer Museum.

Her work is also collected by some of the world’s top collectors, who show her pieces in their private museums. They include Maja Hoffmann’s LUMA Westbau, where she had a show in 2018; François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, where she featured in the 2021 inaugural exhibition and had a solo in 2023; Tony Salamé’s Aishti Foundation in Beirut, which included her in a group show titled “Fresh Flowers”; and a room of work at the Rubell Museum in Miami in 2025.

“We are delighted to begin working with Ser Serpas at this exciting juncture in her growing career,” Hauser & Wirth president Marc Payot said in a statement. “Like a number of our gallery’s foundational artists—Mike Kelley and Jason Rhoades come to mind—she is fearless in her commitment to a process-based, intermedia practice that mingles the deceptively mundane with something powerfully existential. We are excited to embrace her vision and look forward to sharing it with wider audiences.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For this Spirited Away material study, I chose the gate scene from the film’s opening: Chihiro’s father drives the family along a forest road in a 4WD sedan, pushes through overgrown branches and stops in front of a tunnel-like gateway that marks the boundary between the everyday world and the spirit realm.

After they step out of the car, the camera holds on what they see – a weathered red facade, a dark arch, mossy stone, aged wood, and bright summer foliage. That moment is what I rebuilt using Substance 3D Designer and Marmoset. You may also want one of the best laptops for 3D modelling.

I start with a film still of the gate and treat it as the brief. Then I break the shot into texture elements – plaster, wood, tiles, stone, glass, moss – and blueprint how they will sit on the model.

This means sorting trim UVs into a clear texture layout and deciding which textures I actually need before I open Substance Designer.

Sources indicate that next, I author the textures and a few variants so that wear and colour can shift without rebuilding everything. I refine the mesh with height displacement and clean up the trim pieces so the UVs match the strategy.

Finally, I drop in decals for chips, stains, and small story details that make the gate feel lived in.

I bring the textures and models into Marmoset Toolbag and light the scene to echo the film still, encompassing warm daylight, soft shadows and that dark arch in the process.

The last pass involves grading and small post tweaks so that the image stays close to the reference without losing any material clarity.

According to recent reports, it’s a challenge to recreate this movie scene into 3D; perspectives are hand-drawn by Ghibli’s artists, so they’re not necessarily accurate in a 3D sense. I indeed used some tricks to better fit models so they almost match the movie scene.

This process for me is important to recreate the awesome composition of the movie scene.

Roof tile material with a heigh tmap for displacing the mesh. Notice the colour patches in some of the tiles; their final position within the texture is decided while I’m tweaking the final look of the scene in Marmoset Toolbag to better mimic the feeling of the original movie scene.

For the wall component on the ground floor, I made one material with gate hole on it to catch a subtle damage look on the rim of the hole and a variant of that material that tiles horizontally to fill the rest of the wall. This process can be replaced by just using one wall material with decals to do the damage work.

Decals are also fully procedurally generated. I made much of the wall damage into atlas material, because it’s much easier for me to manually place wall damage decals on the wall to match the original movie scene.

Did a Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveal White House Plans to Revamp the Smithsonian?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Smithsonian Institution, which runs a network of nearly two dozen museums and research institutes throughout the United States, has been a target for president Donald Trump throughout his second term.
  • Now, nonprofit newsroom ProPublica has published a report saying that a man on a commuter train heading to Washington, D.C.—apparently a White House staffer—was seen working on a strategy to drastically revamp the policies of Smithsonian Institution museums, including the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, in the nation’s capital, which has repeatedly come in for scrutiny.
  • In a recent development, the evidence?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Smithsonian Institution, which runs a network of nearly two dozen museums and research institutes throughout the United States, has been a target for president Donald Trump throughout his second term. The president and his staffers have criticized Smithsonian policies and challenged museum leaders, including hauling them to the Capitol to submit to openly hostile questioning from elected officials.

Now, nonprofit newsroom ProPublica has published a report saying that a man on a commuter train heading to Washington, D.C.—apparently a White House staffer—was seen working on a strategy to drastically revamp the policies of Smithsonian Institution museums, including the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, in the nation’s capital, which has repeatedly come in for scrutiny. Related Articles Trump Accepts Artistic Gift from India Just Months After Branding it a 'Hellhole' Country The Secret Handshake's Latest Statue Mocks President Trump for Toe-Related Deferment to Avoid Vietnam War Draft.

In a recent development, the evidence? Another commuter’s photos of the staffer’s laptop, snapped over the man’s shoulder as he worked on it in the last week of October.

Sources indicate that the “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan” comprises 25 items. They range from questioning specific exhibits the institution has organized to proposing to rewrite educational materials for schoolchildren and reviewing financial arrangements.

One item deals with a proposed permanent exhibit, to be titled “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and another on “Great Families of American History.” Outside the institution, says the document, should stand a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington.

It has been revealed that fresh: A commuter spotted a blueprint to overhaul the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History while commuting on a crowded Metro train. They sent us photos of the list. Here’s what’s what we learned: https://t.co/XEs8J7zmqO.

The plan also refers to upcoming interpretative guidelines for exhibits and promises a review of the Smithsonian’s “strategy” for traveling exhibitions; it specifically names one, “The Bias Inside Us,” that explores implicit bias and toured the US from early 2021 through summer 2026.

Recent findings suggest that trump has called museums “the last bastion of ‘woke,’” and that buzzword appears in the planning document, which proposes a review of the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. (That organization released a statement with policy proposals for a Democratically dominated Congress the day after the midterm elections.) “AAM helps museums across the country serve the public through professional standards, training, research, and advocacy, and we stand behind that work,” a press representative for AAM told ARTnews in an email. “We do not receive any grants from the Smithsonian Institution.”.

Industry observers note that educational materials for school children also come in for review. The plan proposes overhauling the history museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” Out: a module on immigration called “Becoming US”; in: a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”.

The staffer was also working on a sheet of paper that bore other ideas, such as “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” ProPublica indicates that the latter likely referred to an exhibit on gay history that included a piece of paraphernalia associated with sadomasochistic sex, which was cited in the July report and the hearings that followed.

According to the initials displayed on the staffer’s laptop, ProPublica has determined that the staffer is most likely Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced a lengthy critique of the Smithsonian, published on July 4, that, among other allegations, accused history museum director Anthea Hartig of promoting “an ideological agenda contradictory to the museum’s founding purpose of fostering patriotism.”.

The White House press office did not immediately respond to ARTnews’s request for information on the document or the staffer.

UPDATE, November 23, 1:30 p.m.: This article was updated with a statement from the American Alliance of Museums.

#103435. With MoMA, M+, and the Centre Pompidou’s Alliance, Museums Enter a New Era of Collaboration

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1141 w)

With MoMA, M+, and the Centre Pompidou’s Alliance, Museums Enter a New Era of Collaboration

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you are one of the world’s leading museums of modern and contemporary art, the story you are expected to tell has become global.
  • In the blink of an eye, it seems, the aperture of attention has snapped open to latest world regions, publics, and technologies.
  • Sources indicate that how do you keep up?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you are one of the world’s leading museums of modern and contemporary art, the story you are expected to tell has become global.

In the blink of an eye, it seems, the aperture of attention has snapped open to latest world regions, publics, and technologies. Old narratives are yielding to a liberating, all-embracing polyphony. But this new story demands more, and different, art. Adding to the challenge, art prices are soaring, and so are operating expenses. As the museum pushes into the 21st century, reconfigured as a more open and inclusive enterprise, it must satisfy a host of novel and costly demands. Related Articles MoMA Looks First US Ana Mendieta Retrospective in Nearly 25 Years for 2027 MoMA Shells Out $200,000 for Inaugural Ambasz Prize for 'Nature-Reconciled' Architecture, Half of Which Will Go To Plant Trees.

Sources indicate that how do you keep up? You team up. That’s what Latest York’s Museum of Modern Art, Hong Kong’s M+, and Paris’s Centre Pompidou are doing. Announcing their new tricontinental alliance on October 30, they pledged to treat their collections as one. They are not tinkering around the edges. They are going into the heart of what it means to be a museum. Their goal is to kick the old habit of doing things by yourself, for yourself.

According to recent reports, why would institutions consider such a deep strategic alliance, and why now? Maximizing and leveraging the reach of individual collections is only the start. Museums are painfully aware that their current operating model is under strain. Governments, broke and distracted, are dialing back support. Philanthropy, generally still an American exception, has its own limitations. Earned revenues have plateaued. The room to maneuver is narrow. Doing more with less has become a shared predicament and imperative.

That’s the economic argument. But there’s more. Museum-making, like science, has become a truly international endeavor. Now that so many voices are entering the conversation about art history, it’s best to tap different points of view and realms of expertise. Collaboration, in short, is good not just for efficiency, but for better outcomes.

Industry observers note that institutions already share exhibition development costs and revenues, and co-acquisitions are becoming routine. In state-run systems, clusters of museums sometimes share centralized services such as storage, conservation, and marketing. One member of the upcoming consortium, the Centre Pompidou, already has a constellation network stretching from Belgium to China. Other museums are also teaming up. Earlier this month, the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Shanghai Museum confirmed their commitment to foster “deeper collaboration between the two institutions, including exhibitions, research initiatives, and curatorial exchange.”.

Even so, there is enormous field-wide replication of effort. For the tripartite alliance, research and curatorial collaboration are likely to be just the tip of the iceberg.

Industry observers note that as it happens, I wrote these words from one of the nodes in the partnership, Hong Kong, while participating in the M+ Academy, a upcoming professional development program for museum leaders in the Asia-Pacific region that my firm helped develop. Our meetings were proof positive of the value of closer dialogue and coordination. Each day, we stumbled on new opportunities. Ideas were hatched, arguments sharpened, policies debated. Crucially, in this people-to-people business, we cemented bonds of familiarity and trust. One day, that may translate into loans and projects that would not otherwise have been conceived of, let alone greenlighted.

Some benefits of the alliance are already evident. On a recent busy Sunday, as thousands of visitors crammed into M+ on its fifth birthday, a basement gallery resonated with Janet Cardiff’s acoustic masterpiece, The Forty Part Motet (2001), a long-term loan from MoMA. The Hong Kong curators, meanwhile, are making plans for an M+ capsule gallery to be unveiled inside MoMA next year.

It has been revealed that M+ director Suhanya Raffel sees the roots of the alliance in a decentered art world. “Today, we are all aware how collaboration can add to our cultural authority in various places,” she told me. “This authority is explicit to our audiences, our donors, our corporate partners, the media, our peers, and finally, one hopes, our politicians.” The sustained partnership, if it goes beyond public pronouncements, promises to subtly alter the institutions. Its results will be measured not only in economies of scale, but in fresh undertakings, and perhaps innovative models for museum-making.

Sources indicate that none of which is to downplay the difficulties. The nuts and bolts of managing and building collections are exceedingly complex. So is the diplomacy around museum exchanges, with many spoken and unspoken considerations and crisscrossing commitments in play. Institutional cultures are harder to blend than collections.

It has been revealed that what will success look like? Ultimately, it would mean collections that complement, rather than duplicate, one another. Such integration presumably will mean that one day, a partner institution may pass on an acquisition because another already has rich holdings of the artist in question. But is that realistic? Getting to that place of mutual decision-making will, at best, take time.

For other museums in the US and elsewhere, the announcement sets an example and creates a permission structure to look beyond localized ways of working. In many cities, cultural institutions struggle alone on opposite ends of town, competing for the same pool of visitors, trustees, and money. Their autonomous structure creates few incentives to band together.

Sources indicate that this is one reason why the Toledo Museum of Art has initiated (with my firm’s involvement) a network of museums across the American Midwest to share costs, expertise, and programming, and to explore upcoming ways of working. Bilateral partnerships can pave the way to more ambitious systemwide collaboration. But for now, such strategic operating alliances—let alone full-blown mergers of the sort we are now seeing in higher education— remain vanishingly rare. The integration of New York’s PS1 into MoMA and of the Neue Gallery into the Met are welcome exceptions to the rule.

On the last day of the M+ Academy, our group boarded a bus to Shenzhen, on the Chinese Mainland, where a museum-building boom is in full swing. At the Róng Museum of Art—still a construction site, but already festooned with thousands of digital lanterns on its undulating façades—we met the director, Pi Li, a veteran of M+.

According to recent reports, the conversation promptly turned to how the museum will fill its galleries. The answer was obvious: Institutions across Asia and in the rapidly evolving Global South are hungry to collaborate, chiefly by bringing in exhibitions from more established counterparts. For museums willing to share and open up, a golden age of alliance-building may await.

András Szántó Ph.D., whose most recent book is The Future of the Art World: 38 Dialogues, is the founder of the Fresh York–based cultural strategy firm András Szántó LLC.

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Recent findings suggest that an occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Sources indicate that diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Recent findings suggest that once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

According to office pod brand Framery, when companies resize or move, desks and meeting-room furniture often aren’t deemed “worth the cost of moving” and are discarded during the process.

Framery explained that the EU and US discard 11 million tonnes of furniture a year.

Specifically, the brand points to a study for the European Environmental Bureau, which found that in the EU, 80 to 90 per cent of office furniture is burned or landfilled.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency, in the US, less than one per cent is recycled.

Framery aims to tackle this concern with its office pod subscription service, presenting a more environmentally-friendly alternative to disposing of office furniture when a lease runs out, for example.

“The ‘fast furniture’ trend means 80 per cent of furniture ends up in landfills,” stated Framery’s chief design officer, Joonas Vartola. “We wanted to create a pod that’s part of the solution, not the problem.”.

“Framery pods are built for heavy use, keeping them in the field for tens of thousands of sessions and out of landfills,” Vartola added.

For example, if there’s an increase in staff and more pods are needed, or if an office’s layout changes.

The scheme covers the full range of its signature line pods, from one-person phone booths to meeting pods.

According to Saija Serpola, managing director and founding partner at IR Partners, using the pods has enabled increased flexibility and reduced financial risk when investing in additional office furniture.

“We can terminate, increase, or change the solution as our organisation develops.”.

Framery pods are built from mono-materials, including steel, aluminium, glass and PET.

In a recent development, “Our pods with heavy-duty, high-quality materials engineered to withstand wear and tear,” stated Vartola. “It’s all about reducing waste, from design to decades of use.”.

As part of the scheme, when a change is required, the pods are dismantled, shipped and rebuilt, rather than discarded into landfill.

Industry observers note that according to Framery, each pod is designed for disassembly, with all parts replaceable and recyclable. This includes everything from interior panels, glass, upholstery, carpet, ventilation units and seals.

During refurbishment, each pod is restored to as-new condition and delivered to its next office with a lifetime warranty.

“That is a manufacturing question before it is a commercial one, and it is settled years earlier, on the drawing board.”.

To learn more, visit Framery’s website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the first thing I noticed about GTA 6’s interface was how much it felt like GTA. That sounds obvious, but it's a massive design achievement to keep the same series going for 25 years and ensure the UI and HUD feel familiar while still developing new visual quirks.

My first impressions of the HUD from my time reviewing GTA 6 were familiar but evolved just enough: the same icons in the same places, but sharper and more refined, with in-game apps and the character's phone. That’s no accident. Rockstar’s UI team has spent the game’s development working out how to keep the series’ look while making it feel fresh.

Industry observers note that “Almost 25 years ago, we helped bring Vice City to life,” says Stuart Petri, Vice President of Art: 2D/UI Design. What began as “a simple visual design language”, he says, has become “far more sophisticated, layered, and considered”.

It has been revealed that the team's challenge was to make the UI and HUD “feel fresh, contemporary, and relevant for a new generation, while retaining the heritage that makes it unmistakably GTA”. Petri points to the visual signatures that connect past and present: the iconic Pricedown font, the familiar minimap, the wanted stars and the Wasted screen.

Recent findings suggest that the interface also needs to know when to disappear. “It should be there when you need it, but at the same time is not distracting,” Petri indicates. “A single press of a button gets you what you need, then back to the game and it’s gone.”.

Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of customisation options too, from making the mini-map larger, dynamic, or even adding a top-of-the-screen compass or removing it all. The default UI is balanced and riffs on past GTA games: a small map, subtle police ratings, and small health bars.

His summary is short: “Twenty-five years on, the DNA remains.”.

Sam Grosset, Associate UI Director, UI/UX Design, claims the team wants the UI to feel “like a natural extension of the game world, supporting players without interrupting gameplay or breaking immersion, unless necessary to do so”.

The biggest example is the phone. “It was a big shift for our phone interface to be in-hand,” Grosset states, “but it supports that feeling of playing as Jason or Lucia and helps us stay embedded in the world.”.

The phone is a tap away, but feels connected to the UI design, layered in humour – BuckMe and RydeMe apps or the Waink app to scan and record the world, all help make GTA very modern and typically Rockstar all at once.

Grosset claims accessibility was “considered from the outset”, and that “designing for diverse needs enables us to create better games for everyone”.

Industry observers note that in practice, he states, that means options such as “selecting a larger font size, opting for a more minimal screen experience, or making a controls tweak to sprinting”. Rockstar wants every player to have options to play the game how they like, so if you want the classic experience, it's here, but if you want more assists, those are here too. And I don't regret losing the ability to tap a button to run for a second (though bikes still have the old input).

Recent findings suggest that mark Tennant, Vice President of Animation, says the physical side of the partnership needed “a lot of thought and iteration”. Players can interact with their partner in “a natural, loving way”, with “a believable progression based on their overall investment in the relationship”.

The animators had to find “a realistic balance between player agency and partner response while keeping things fun, passionate, and rewarding”, Tennant says.

All of that sits on top of the everyday stuff. Tennant says there are “close to a thousand animation sets for ambient activities”, plus “hundreds of bespoke one-off events and custom sequences”. Keeping them consistent meant working closely with the design team across the whole world.

You’ll never consciously notice most of it. But when a character can’t open a door without bumping a hip, it’s a sign Rockstar wants you to feel the weight of Leonida.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance.
  • According to recent reports, creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells.
  • Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

According to recent reports, creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

According to recent reports, now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a massive-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

Recent findings suggest that so, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s notable to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

Recent findings suggest that the same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Industry observers note that does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

According to recent reports, some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Industry observers note that beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Industry observers note that thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health complications that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

In a recent development, creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

Friedrich Christian Flick, Art Collector and Scion of German Industrialists with Nazi Past, Dies at 82

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Friedrich Christian Flick, a major collector of contemporary art and scion to one of Germany’s wealthiest industrialist families, died at 82 in Rosenheim in southern Germany.
  • Flick was a fixture of ARTnews Top 200 Collectors in the early 2000s, appearing on the list consecutively from 1999 to 2007.
  • According to recent reports, his patronage of the arts was not without controversy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Friedrich Christian Flick, a major collector of contemporary art and scion to one of Germany’s wealthiest industrialist families, died at 82 in Rosenheim in southern Germany. Flick died after suffering injuries from a fall days earlier, according to Monopol magazine.

Flick was a fixture of ARTnews Top 200 Collectors in the early 2000s, appearing on the list consecutively from 1999 to 2007. Flick’s collection is comprised of some 2,500 works, including major pieces by Bruce Nauman, Alberto Giacometti, Marcel Duchamp, Gerhard Richter, Georg Baselitz, Paul McCarthy, and Martin Kippenberger. Related Articles Top 200 Collector Mitchell Rales Gifts $116 M. to National Gallery of Art for Lending Program Newsmakers: Carmen Reviriego on Patronage, Power, and the Future of Spain's Cultural Funding.

According to recent reports, his patronage of the arts was not without controversy. His grandfather, Friedrich Flick, who died in 1972, was a top arms supplier to Nazi Germany and had built his company, which included production of coal and steel, on forced labor.

It has been revealed that in 2001, Flick hired Rem Koolhaas to design a newly introduced museum to house the collection in Zurich. The project was met with protests both from writers and artists, as well as major Jewish groups, who criticized Flick for not contributing to a $6 billion fund for survivors of slave labor factories like those run by his grandfather.

The museum project was abandoned, and in 2003, Flick sought a upcoming path for showing the works from the collection through a partnership with the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which operates Berlin’s museums. Flick loaned the collection for seven years to Hamburger Bahnhof museum and paid to renovate a 19th-century warehouse into an annex for the museum, as the New York Times reported at the time. According to Monopol, Flick also commissioned the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation to conduct research into his family’s Nazi past, founded a foundation against xenophobia and racism, and donated €5 million to the forced labor fund.

Industry observers note that those moves did little to quell the controversy. In a 2004 op-ed for Handelsblatt, a German business newspaper, Salomon Korn, the vice president of Germany’s Central Council of Jews, called the deal “a kind of whitewashing of blood money into a socially accepted form of art property.” In an open letter, Korn asked further, “Will there soon be a ‘Göring Collection’ in Berlin?”.

Per Monopol, Flick later said the response “deeply distressed” him, but that it “forced me to grapple with my family history.” Still, in a 2004 interview with NPR, Flick argued that his family’s Nazi past should not be presented with the works in collection.

“My family history led me to collect works from the kinds of artists who ask irritating questions and challenge people,” he stated. “But the family story has to be separated from the presentation of the collection. It would abuse the artwork to present it in the context of my family history. The art is not there for that. It stands on its own.”.

It has been revealed that the partnership between Flick and the Hamburger Bahnhof continued until 2021, when the halls renovated by Flick to house his art were sold off to a private real estate company, which decided to demolish them. Some of Flick’s works remain on view elsewhere in Berlin: In 2008 and 2014, Flick donated 268 works, including pieces by McCarthy, Pipilotti Rist, Stan Douglas, and others, to the National Gallery. It is not yet clear what will happen to the rest of the collection.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, spain’s National Police have spent the past 47 years searching for a Romanesque wood carving of the Virgin Mary that was stolen from the Church of Sa Pedro de Meoz in Navarre, part of the Basque area of northern Spain. At last, they finally found it.

The 21-inch-tall gilded object was nabbed by the notorious “gentleman thief” René Alphonse van den Berghe, known as Erik the Belgian, who robbed churches and monasteries in rural Spain in the late 1970s and early ’80s. Many of his marks have since been recovered. In 2023, for example, a missing fragment from a set of six 17th-century Flemish tapestries was returned to the church in Castrojeriz, Spain, from where Erik the Belgian had swiped them in 1980. Related Articles Stolen Picasso Prints Found Under Pile of Clothes in French Riviera Apartment Police Recover Three Religious Artworks Stolen From Spanish Churches.

As reported in El País, the investigation leading to this latest discovery picked up steam in April. The authorities knew that Erik the Belgian transported most of his loot from Spain to other European countries “with higher demand in the art and antiques market.”.

The local paper Noticias de Navarra notes that in 2012 the Virgin sculpture was sold by a Belgian antique dealer named Bernard Descheemaker, and that by 2017 it was part of the collection Daniel Kanz Gallery in London.

In 2020, according to El País, it found its way to Maastricht in the Netherlands as part of TEFAF, the prestigious art and antiques fair organized by the European Fine Art Foundation. It then “passed through the hands of various antique dealers and collectors,” eventually landing with a Spanish art collection in the UK.

The handover took place at the Spanish Embassy in London, and the piece is now back in Spain.

  • Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Industry observers note that feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:.

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future aims feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

Industry observers note that if imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love looks a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Industry observers note that remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Industry observers note that shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

According to recent reports, no respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

According to recent reports, if they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Sources indicate that still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Recent findings suggest that are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.

Central to the building’s new function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.

“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts noted.

“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”.

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS remarked this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “vital conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

On Monday, Vogue US and British Vogue published their lists simultaneously, featuring A-list stars such as Zendaya, Kendall Jenner, Greta Lee, Sarah Pidgeon and more. Artists were also named, although few and far among them were British painter and writer Lynette Yiadom-Boakye, artist and choreographer Anne Imhof, and architect Sumayya Vally.

Industry observers note that vogue US selected 55 individuals for its best-dressed lists, while British Vogue handpicked 50. Yiadom-Boakye and Vally made it to British Vogue’s list, and Imhof was paired with her partner, the dancer Devon Teuscher, by Vogue US. Imhof and Teuscher were described as “Berghain Romeo and Juliet” by Vogue US, and the publication said 2026 was their year because of Imhof’s queer, Shakespearean solo exhibition “House of Swans,” which features a four-act ballet. Last year’s Vogue US list featured artist and Newly introduced York’s First Lady Rama Duwaji. Vogue US could not be reached for a comment at time of publication.

In a recent development, british Vogue’s best-dressed list applauded Yiadom-Boakye for her “eclectic” style. The magazine compared the artist’s style to the characters featured in her portraits, where “clothes naturally play a crucial role,” but argued that “while the fashion that features in her art never feels too hooked to a particular time or place, the clothes in her real-world wardrobe couldn’t feel more now.”.

Another name on the list was Vally, the architect who will be designing French-Lebanese philanthropist Elie Khouri’s contemporary art foundation, the Elie Khouri Art Foundation. The magazine described Vally as “hardly your typical fashion girlie” and that her signature look is her “slinky, head-to-toe black and statement winged eyeliner.” The architect is also a fixture on the front row of runway demonstrates, from Hermès to Roksanda and Harris Reed. British Vogue could not be reached for a comment at time of publication.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Faurschou Newly introduced York opened in 2019, the New York Times compared it to major collector-founded institutions like the Hill Art Foundation, the FLAG Art Foundation, and the Brant Foundation. But unlike those institutions, Faurschou New York was not a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. It also never quite lived up to its lofty expectations.

It has been revealed that in March 2025, Faurschou, which was founded as a private art museum and art consultancy in Copenhagen in 1986, revealed that the New York outpost was closed “for renovations.” It never reopened. The Greenpoint building that housed it was sold in June to a developer, city records show, and the city has approved its demolition. A condominium planned for the site cements what founder and art collector Jens Faurschou himself announced in April: After four decades, Faurschou’s public exhibitions are over. Related Articles Lynette Yiadom-Boakye and Anne Imhof Make Vogue's 2026 Best-Dressed List 13th-Century Carving Stolen by Art Thief 'Eric the Belgian' Recovered in the UK.

It has been revealed that the building at 148-150 Green Street, once home to Faurschou Upcoming York and the restaurant Ilis, was sold at the end of June to the developer Investmates for $25.55 million, according to city property records reviewed by ARTnews. The seller, Green Art Holdings LLC, bought it in 2017 for $18 million, according to Commercial Observer. On October 27, the Department of Buildings approved its full demolition, according to city records. Investmates aims a seven-story, 73-unit condominium on the site, Crain’s reported.

According to recent reports, in a statement posted to the company’s website, Jens Faurschou remarked that with the closing of the Newly introduced York space he was “bringing the public exhibition program to an end.” After 40 years, he wrote, his “direction changes”: He will focus on his family, private dealing, and working with artists, institutions, and collections. The statement does not clarify what will become of the collection, or whether the Copenhagen and Beijing spaces remain operational.

Faurschou staged solo exhibitions of artists from Tracey Emin to Shirin Neshat and Danh Vo, and highlighted works by Robert Rauschenberg and Louise Bourgeois. Programming at its global locations appeared to have stopped years earlier: Copenhagen last listed an exhibition in 2018 and Beijing in 2021-22, according to the firm’s website and exhibition listings.

Its 12,000-square-foot New York space last hosted an exhibition of work by the Chinese artist Ai Weiwei, which ended in February 2025. As of late October 2025, the exhibition appeared to still be installed, visible through the windows. Neither the artist’s studio nor Faurschou responded to a request for comment at that time.

His statement did not address the tech giant’s finances, which have come under scrutiny in recent years. An auditor warned about its accounts, and a court issued a bankruptcy order against Faurschou ApS in November 2025 that was canceled two weeks later.

According to recent reports, A degree of mystery surrounds the Danish art dealer, dubbed the “Don Corleone of art” in a 2016 Politiken profile. By his account, his career began in 1984, the year he traveled to Fresh York City and made his first art deal—a few Fluxus works, sold at the suggestion of Art Library founder Knud Pedersen. That same year, he met his future first wife, Luise Faurschou. The two married in 1985 and soon after opened Galleri Faurschou on Store Strandstræde.

Industry observers note that according to the profile, the gallery maintained a small but respectable stable of artists—Christian Lemmerz, Nina Sten-Knudsen, Erik A. Frandsen, and Michael Kvium—while also handling blue-chip works. “I sold Warhol,” he recalled. “I sold Poliakoff, I sold Picasso, lots of Picassos. The biggest deal I made, which was the most fun, was around 2004. It was a package of five Picassos and two Mirós.” In 2012, he and Luise relocated the business to Nordhavn, which he continued to run alone following their divorce.

The Faurschou collection underpins his business, but in interviews, he has declined to specify its scope, value, and exact ownership. In 2016, he compared himself to collectors who “have a showroom and a massive collection. And sell something from time to time to be able to buy something else.” He claimed to have purchased a monumental work from Robert Rauschenberg, which he said he would part with only for the Museum of Modern Art in New York. (There is no public record that MoMA owns a Rauschenberg that was sold or donated by Jens Faurschou. However, Mirthday Man, a work from the Faurschou collection, was shown in a 2017 Rauschenberg exhibition at MoMA.).

According to recent reports, also listed in his collection are works by Louise Bourgeois, Cai Guo-Qiang, Danh Vo, Shirin Neshat, and Bill Viola, as well as a substantial number of pieces by Ai Weiwei. He told Politiken the value of the collection “depends on whether it’s a good or a bad day,” and that he is an art dealer but that he “no longer” runs a gallery that represents artists and sells their works.

A 2024 article in the Danish-language outlet Børsen described Faurschou’s business model as including a “philanthropic” part, which stages “non-commercial” exhibitions. His philanthropic activities, the report notes, include helping establish the art center and nonprofit organization Copenhagen Contemporary. When he opened his Brooklyn location in 2019, Faurschou told the Upcoming York Times that he occasionally sells works from his private collection and does consulting work to finance his free exhibitions. According to Børsen, however, his business is financed by wealthy, unnamed individuals, who also finance and own the art. In 2025, Jyllands-Posten estimated that the collection comprises roughly 400 works.

Recent findings suggest that faurschou has mentioned that these non-commercial shows have cost him several million DKK over the years. The Politiken profile notes that several of Faurschou’s companies narrowly sidestepped going into the red in 2015, after the sale of several properties in Taastrup. The art dealer said he was “absolutely” generating funds from the collection to remedy the shortfall.

In a recent development, jyllands-Posten reported in 2025 that with a loss exceeding DKK 25 million ($3.6 million) in 2024, his holding manufacturer, Faurschou Holding ApS, had amassed total losses of nearly DKK 174 million ($25.3 million) since its founding in 2012. Company accounts show equity has been negative for six straight years, standing at a deficit of DKK 154 million ($22.4 million) as of 2024. Given these circumstances, the auditor expressed doubts about the value of the art Faurschou has purchased, noting that there was “significant uncertainty about the valuation of the company’s assets.”.

The 2023 accounts were similarly fraught. Børsen reported in 2024 that despite his industry renown, “the seasoned art dealer has blood-red accounts, where virtually no values are registered.” Faurschou also had a dispute with an auditor from Deloitte, who at the time questioned his business model. According to the article, the auditor wrote that the organization accounts “do not give a true and fair view of the companies’ liabilities, assets and financial position, and in addition, the auditor does not believe in the companies’ future operations.”.

The report added: “Because there is no faith in the future operations, the auditor also calls the management report incorrect, as it assumes continued operations.”.

It has been revealed that this credit history painted a tense backdrop for the company’s brush with bankruptcy. On November 6, 2025, the Probate Court of the Maritime and Commercial Court in Denmark issued a bankruptcy order for Faurschou ApS, only to cancel it on November 20. The cancelation ended the legal process that would have seized the company’s assets and operations, because the legal threshold for bankruptcy was no longer met.

It has been revealed that public records also show legal claims on Faurschou’s own property. Notices in Statstidende say Møns Bank asked a court to auction two properties he owns, a house in Humlebæk and a summer house in Nysted, with sales set for May. As of November 23, the land registry still listed him as the owner of the Humlebæk house. Separately, the registry shows the Danish Tax Administration placed liens on that house on April 23 totaling about DKK 8.5 million, or roughly $1.3 million.

Recent findings suggest that for his part, Faurschou had expressed confidence in the future of his tech giant, telling Børsen in 2024: “I have tried to explain to the accountant why I see it differently than he does, but I absolutely cannot blame him for what he writes, because the requirements for an accountant are much higher today than they were before.” He mentioned the company was working on “large and complex projects,” the details of which he could not share at the time. He added that, alongside the “philanthropic” part of his business, there was an “income-generating” side, where he acted as a broker for major art dealers and facilitated sales from the company’s collection. His April statement does not indicate whether his prepares to focus on private dealing include that brokerage and those collection sales.

Reports have left unclear the exact nature of Faurschou’s operations, and the terms used to describe it have shifted over the years between “foundation” and “private museum.”.

“You call [Faurschou] a foundation, but it’s not a trust, is it,” Politiken asked. Faurschou replied, “No, but neither is the Tryg Foundation,” referencing the charitable arm of TryghedsGruppen, a Danish holding company that is the largest shareholder of the insurance company Tryg. He confirmed that his business is a limited company and explained that the use of the word “foundation” signals that the art on view is not for sale. Visitors “expect to come into a place where there [are] no sales” being conducted, he noted, adding that this also ensured employees at the front desk were not asked about the price list.

When pressed further, he stressed that at least the Copenhagen operation “absolutely” was philanthropic, but did not elaborate on the specifics of the philanthropy. “It’s just that not many people take advantage of the philanthropic offer,” he said.

Faurschou rolled out its Greenpoint, Brooklyn, space in 2019 to great fanfare. Mads Refslund, the Scandinavian chef who cofounded Copenhagen’s Noma with René Redzepi, opened Ilis Newly introduced York in a space attached to Faurschou. (Refslund is reportedly close with Jens Faurschou and his wife, Marsha, with one source saying he contributed to their wedding menu.) The opening of Ilis, packed with art world regulars, was similarly tasteful: employees’ uniforms were designed by Camilla Staerk and Lady and Butler’s founder Eli Caner. The restaurant closed in May 2026, citing the building’s sale; Refslund told Eater that he and a group of investors had tried to buy the building, but were outbid by a developer.

In his closing remark, Jens Faurschou described the whole venture, across four cities, as a “program of cross-cultural dialogue.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
