  • According to recent reports, A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people.
  • Industry observers note that in fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb.
  • If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

Industry observers note that in fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas, tells SELF. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.).

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran states. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

It has been revealed that if you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication right about now. Pollen counts are rising, and antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

It has been revealed that both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller notes. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.).

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran claims. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she indicates.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller states. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off.
  • According to recent reports, many of these skin concerns get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine.
  • But if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off. It’s normal to experience some skin issues from time to time, like itchiness, breakouts, or ingrown hairs. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign that something more serious is going on.

According to recent reports, many of these skin concerns get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine. For example, if dryness pops up when Old Man Winter comes along, slathering on a more intense moisturizer may help.

But if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit. However, just because you have a lasting symptom or two doesn’t necessarily mean you have a chronic health matter.

Here are the symptoms you should watch for and what they might mean. And if they don’t improve, consider checking in with a dermatologist for a proper diagnosis and a strategy of action.

According to recent reports, if you wish you had cat claws to satisfy your skin itch, you could be dealing with eczema. Eczema is an umbrella term for several conditions that impact the skin, with atopic dermatitis being the most common.

With most forms of eczema, your skin may show signs of inflammation, such as:.

These symptoms may flare up occasionally and then go into periods of remission, where your skin isn’t as irritated.

Allergies can also lead to itchiness. For example, if you’re allergic to a skin care ingredient, a fabric type, a pet, or another allergen, your skin might react as a way to tell you to avoid this trigger.

Ongoing or regular periods of itchiness are a reason to see a dermatologist.

A rash can affect the skin in various ways, including:.

Sources indicate that A one-off or temporary rash might result from friction or chafing from a new outfit item. It could also be a heat rash when sweat gets trapped in skinfolds or bodily creases.

Sources indicate that A persistent rash could be a sign of eczema or allergies. However, different types of rashes can be a sign of other things. For example, a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the face is a common sign of an autoimmune disease known as lupus.

If you frequently experience skin rashes, talk with a dermatologist to help you get to the bottom of the glitch.

Dry skin can be just that — dry skin. Common causes include:.

But if your skin is so dry it makes you want to bathe in a vat of thick moisturizer, it could be a sign of psoriasis.

Psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition potentially caused by an overactive immune system. It can lead to dry, cracked, or scaling skin. In fact, psoriasis often involves a buildup of scales or plaques on areas like the elbows or knees — though they can occur anywhere.

Psoriasis and eczema are different conditions, but they have overlapping symptoms that mimic each other. So if you experience these symptoms, it’s crucial to see a dermatologist to identify and treat the underlying cause.

Changes in skin color — including red, brown, gray, or purple patches of skin — can be a sign of various skin issues, including eczema, psoriasis, or allergies. But it can also be a sign of rosacea.

Recent findings suggest that rosacea typically involves persistent redness that looks like a sunburn or blushing. It may also lead to skin thickening.

The good news? Rosacea is highly treatable. So working with a dermatologist can help you address it.

No one is immune from developing the occasional pimple or ingrown hair. But sometimes, skin bumps can be a sign that something else is going on.

Acne is one of the most common skin conditions that could bring skin bumps like pimples.

It has been revealed that hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is another condition that causes painful, boil-like lumps to form underneath the skin. These bumps can turn into pus-filled pockets that may connect via tunnels. HS typically demonstrates up in areas of high friction or where skin meets skin, such as the armpits or groin.

Other types of skin bumps may include ingrown hairs, which can get infected and turn into folliculitis.

Talk with a dermatologist to help you address any bothersome skin bumps you may experience.

Common moles are growths that develop when pigment cells (melanocytes) grow in clusters. The average adult has between 10 to 40 common moles.

An irregular mole, also known as a dysplastic nevus, is a type of mole that looks different from your common moles. If you have a dysplastic nevus (or several), schedule regular skin checks with a dermatologist to look for anything suspicious. Be sure to mention any changes in:.

According to recent reports, these types of changes could be a sign of a form of skin cancer such as melanoma, which occurs in melanocytes. Melanoma can develop anywhere, including on normal-looking skin, a common mole, or a dysplastic nevus.

According to recent reports, skin symptoms — like rashes, bumps, discoloration, dryness, or itchiness — may come and go. But if symptoms stick around or return frequently, consider seeing a dermatologist for an evaluation. Your skin may be telling you that there’s an underlying problem that needs to be addressed.

A dermatologist can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment strategy to help reduce, or, in some cases, resolve your skin symptoms. If you don’t at the moment have a dermatologist, your primary care physician or nurse practitioner can refer you to one.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a LinkedIn post, Williamson noted he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.
  • Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson noted he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he said he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework currently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a fresh regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson mentioned his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

“Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”.

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he stated he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

According to recent reports, it also proposes fresh legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

“I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

Recent findings suggest that “While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”.

Williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.

#103325. 7 Common Misdiagnoses for Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)

📅 14 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (849 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Greatist ↗ Open Full Page

7 Common Misdiagnoses for Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)

📅 14 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (849 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a skin condition that often gets caught up in a case of mistaken identity in a lineup of suspects.
  • Sources indicate that with their host of bumps, rashes, flakiness, or scales, skin conditions can sometimes be tricky to diagnose.
  • Sources indicate that so, what exactly is HS?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a skin condition that often gets caught up in a case of mistaken identity in a lineup of suspects. Specifically, people confuse HS for some more common conditions.

Sources indicate that with their host of bumps, rashes, flakiness, or scales, skin conditions can sometimes be tricky to diagnose. That’s because they often share common symptoms or have symptoms that overlap with or mimic those of another skin concern.

Sources indicate that so, what exactly is HS? It’s a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in friction-prone and sweaty areas, where your skin can be sensitive. These lumps can form interconnected tracts underneath your skin (aka “tunneling”) that may become irritated or even infected.

Knowing how the symptoms of HS compare with those of other inflammatory skin conditions can help you advocate for the correct diagnosis and care, which is crucial for staving off disease progression.

Here are 7 conditions that HS commonly gets mistaken for.

HS isn’t rare — it affects up to 4% of the population. But by comparison, acne vulgaris affects more than more than 9% of people worldwide. Sometimes HS can be mistaken for acne simply because acne is more common. But these two conditions are quite different.

Acne typically reveals up as papules, pustules, or nodules, which are commonly called zits or blemishes. Acne most often appears on your face but can also affect your back, chest, arms, and buttocks. It occurs when your sebaceous glands have a hypersensitivity to circulating androgens (like testosterone).

It has been revealed that by comparison, HS most often appears in sweat- and friction-prone areas, such as your armpits or groin. It occurs when hair follicles become blocked — though more research is needed to learn what causes these blockages.

In a recent development, acne conglobata (AC) is a rare but intense form of nodulocystic acne. With AC, the cysts and nodules connect under your skin, and this can lead to infections and scarring. Since AC features a “tunneling” effect that may appear similar to HS, many people confuse these two otherwise distinct conditions.

One key difference? HS often appears in areas that are subjected to friction from skin-on-skin contact or chafing. AC, on the other hand, can appear anywhere on your body. To further complicate things, many people with HS also have AC, and some research suggests a link between the two conditions.

A cyst is a fluid-filled sac. Cysts have many possible causes, including injuries and minor infections. They often go away on their own, but some may require treatment.

HS bumps can resemble cysts — but HS is an ongoing inflammatory condition.

According to recent reports, an ingrown hair happens when a strand of hair anywhere on your body grows into your skin instead of out. Ingrown hairs commonly occur after shaving, waxing, or tweezing. After hair removal, a tiny new hair can curl inward, creating a bump (often called a razor bump).

It has been revealed that sometimes people confuse HS bumps for ingrown hairs — especially since HS often occurs in places where hair removal is common, such as the armpits and bikini area. Another confusing factor is that HS develops from blocked follicles. However, the cause of the blockage in HS is more complicated than an ingrown hair.

According to recent reports, folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, usually caused by a bacterial infection. The inflamed hair follicles show up as small bumps and can look like ingrown hairs.

People commonly mistake HS for folliculitis because the conditions often occur in the same skin areas.

Mild folliculitis tends to go away on its own with at-home treatment, though more severe forms may require antibiotics. HS, on the other hand, is a chronic condition.

A boil (also called a furuncle) is a bump filled with pus. The bump develops from a bacterial infection, often of a hair follicle. The infection causes a buildup of immune and skin cells, which leads to the formation of the bump. A carbuncle is a cluster of boils.

People often confuse HS with boils. However, boils are the result of an infection, and proper treatment typically resolves the matter. Meanwhile, the boil-like bumps of HS often require ongoing treatment.

Herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the herpes simplex virus. It reveals up as painful sores or blisters.

In a recent development, since herpes often affects the genital area and HS occurs around the groin or bikini line, people may confuse the two conditions. But while herpes can be spread through direct contact, HS is not contagious.

According to recent reports, other skin conditions can mimic HS, and vice versa. But a misdiagnosis can lead to an incorrect treatment that won’t actually ease your symptoms or slow the condition’s progression. This is true for other skin conditions as well.

That’s why, if you have symptoms of any of the above conditions, you should talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can properly diagnose your concerns and find the right treatment proposal.

Industry News: IKEA's Color of the Year "unexpectedly fits in"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).
  • Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.
  • Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of IKEA (unless stated otherwise).

Swedish retailer IKEA has unveiled its prediction for 2027’s Color of the Year – a dark, reddish-purple shade called Wild Fig.

Although revealed by IKEA US as part of its 2027 Style Guide, keen eyes would’ve already seen the shade pop up earlier this year in the sell-out floor lamp created by Dutch designer Lex Pott for IKEA’s PS Collection.

The company describes Wild Fig as “a deep, botanical shade with a rich purple tone”, although in certain lights, it looks closer to an earthy oxblood red.

“Full of character and the unexpected, it brings depth and a daring mindset to everyday spaces,” mentioned Abbey Stark, home furnishing direction leader at IKEA US.

Used across furnishings and accessories, it can provide a subtle touch of colour without being overly aggressive, especially paired with warm woods and neutral shades, IKEA US suggests.

But the company equally pictures it being splashed across entire walls and argues it “unexpectedly fits in” with even brighter colours like baby pink and electric blue – IKEA US’s previous colours of the year.

The tech giant’s Style Guide also pulled out a number of other interior design trends to look out for in 2027, including pattern clashing and Japandi minimalism.

Interior designers have already started making liberal use of Wild Fig, as seen in Note Design Studio’s scheme for the Lammhults showroom in Stockholm, where it blankets walls, floors and ceilings in the entrance, as well as an entire kitchen.

Other predictions for 2027’s colour of the year are set to start rolling in any minute, with Pantone’s set to be unveiled at the start of December.

Paint brand Dulux got ahead of the game when it named a muted green called Soulful Sage as its contender in September.

Some interiors industry insiders, including Dezeen columnist Michelle Ogundehin, have argued at least since the end of the pandemic that “it’s time to reconsider the whole colour of the year carnival”, which was originally invented as a marketing stunt for Pantone’s colour-matching system, much like the Michelin Guide was invented to sell more tyres.

#103322. Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1432 w)

Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1432 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism.
  • Recent findings suggest that the truth?
  • Recent findings suggest that metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

Recent findings suggest that the truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

Recent findings suggest that metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

According to recent reports, in short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, states Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

That remarked, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research highlights that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

In a recent development, this can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

Sources indicate that strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

Sources indicate that by strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

Those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison indicates what’s most key is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

Protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

Protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

It has been revealed that however, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, says doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

For most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That said, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

An often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of issues, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research highlights that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

In a recent development, prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research reveals chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

There is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

Sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.
  • An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.
  • Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in newly introduced directions.”.

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” remarked the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture.

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” noted Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that he saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

Industry observers note that “I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she said. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”.

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually established themselves among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an key influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

It has been revealed that after graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” said Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”.

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” noted Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

Sources indicate that “Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… traveling the world as much as we to can see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”.

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its thought thorugh eclecticism.

“We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he said. “I would say it’s something that it’s very important and it’s gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”.

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”.

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell is size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.

Looking ahead, the architects said their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo remarked there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”.

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto said if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”.

“If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”.

Recent findings suggest that to celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

According to recent reports, situated within a 32-acre university campus, the main administration offices, along with an open-air auditorium, seminar halls, library, and cafeteria, form the functions of Prestige University. The building gradually steps up from the approach, becoming a multifunctional stage for large-scale events, seating 9000 students at a time. Inside, spaces are interspersed with naturally lit landscaped courtyards, allowing indirect light to infuse the internal volumes at each level, creating an energy-efficient, sustainable building with minimal dependence on artificial lighting and air conditioning - responding to a climate that varies from 30°C to 40°C for 8 months of the year. The built form evokes images of stepped wells in India which have existed since 1100 years; spaces not just built to store water but also social interactions bringing the community together.

The tea shop offers neighbourhood belonging and ecological repair to the site. It has been revealed that this neo-natural ocean kelp reef transforms architectural knowledge into botanical DNA. The structure is 3D-printed from calcium carbonate and engineered with porous zones that support kelp attachment and cold-water growth. Within geo-fenced, airtight vitrines, suspended specimens of dried ocean microalgae demonstrate a transgenic process in which texts, images, and drawings are encoded directly into the genetic material of engineered vegetation. The reef operates as a living, photosynthetic library. At planetary scale, the system merges two powerful sinks: carbon sequestration and long-term cold data storage.

#103319. 7 Places on the Body That Hidradenitis Suppurativa Can Appear

📅 28 Feb 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (954 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Greatist ↗ Open Full Page

7 Places on the Body That Hidradenitis Suppurativa Can Appear

📅 28 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that despite what Instagram and photo filters would have us think, no one has perfectly smooth skin over the entirety of their body.
  • But hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is different.
  • In a recent development, HS lumps or bumps can form interconnected tracts underneath the skin that may become inflamed and infected, causing discomfort and pain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that despite what Instagram and photo filters would have us think, no one has perfectly smooth skin over the entirety of their body. We’re all prone to the occasional bump, rash, zit, or ingrown hair. These complications generally go away after the blocked follicle, clogged pore, or minor skin irritation resolves.

But hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is different. HS is a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in some of your most sensitive regions (and beyond).

In a recent development, HS lumps or bumps can form interconnected tracts underneath the skin that may become inflamed and infected, causing discomfort and pain. Although infections are often a part of HS, the disease itself is not an infection — it’s due to an ongoing inflammatory response in the body.

In addition to causing pain and discomfort, HS can be extremely frustrating and impact your self-esteem. Identifying HS correctly and early is crucial for getting optimal care, easing symptoms, slowing disease progression, and improving your mental health.

According to recent reports, while we don’t know what exactly causes HS, genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors may play a role. Skin regions prone to HS include those where we sweat often and where friction is super common. Friction can occur from skin rubbing on skin, or where clothing can chafe or rub.

Here are seven areas of the body that are often impacted by HS.

Recent findings suggest that our underarms are packed with hair follicles and apocrine glands (aka, sweat glands). With HS, these follicles and glands may become clogged, and bacteria can start to grow, leading to the inflamed boil-like bumps of HS.

In a recent development, if you’ve ever gone for a run and come back with the dreaded armpit chafing, you’re all too familiar with how this area of the body can be prone to skin-on-skin friction or excessive rubbing from clothing. (Lookin’ at you, sports bra!) Friction and chafing can also cause an HS flare-up.

In a recent development, complicating matters is that some people shave or wax their armpits, and many understandably slather this region with antiperspirants or deodorants. These factors can also clog or irritate sweat glands and hair follicles.

The breasts, including underneath and even on the areolae (the area around the nipple), are a common place for HS to show up.

Industry observers note that the breast area is a frequent spot for chafing from bras or other clothing. This chafing not only causes skin irritation — it can also trap sweat and bacteria on the skin. The areolae contain apocrine glands and hair follicles that can easily become infected. All these factors can contribute to an HS flare.

Research also points to sex hormones playing a role in HS, so a hormone shift or imbalance may also make breast tissue more prone to HS lesions. However, more research is needed on the connection between HS and hormones.

In a recent development, no one can deny that the crotch becomes a sweaty area when life gets steamy, either from the weather, a workout, or both. It’s also a common area for clothing to rub against just from walking and everyday movements.

As with other HS-prone areas, the groin and genital areas contain apocrine glands and oodles of hair follicles, all of which can become blocked as part of HS, leading to a flare. Speaking of hair down there, many people groom their pubic region, which can also lead to blocked hair follicles.

Again, hormonal shifts or imbalances may also play a role in why these sensitive areas can become hot spots for HS.

The inner thighs are an extension of the groin area. Similarly, sweat also hangs out here, and it’s a common spot for chafing to occur from skin-on-skin friction, or from clothing rubbing and irritating the area.

The entire buttocks area is also prone to HS in many people. Areas commonly affected include the anus, the butt crack, and the gluteal fold — or the crease where the buttocks meet the backs of the upper thighs.

Apocrine glands and hair follicles are abundant here, too. Sweat and other bacteria sources can also lead to HS infections. The buttocks are also subjected to pressure from sitting, which can lead to further irritation.

Although more research is needed, some studies suggest a link between HS and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). IBD is an umbrella term for conditions such as Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis. The potential links between HS and IBD may play a role in why the buttocks area is a common site for HS.

Industry observers note that although less common than in other areas, HS can also show up at the nape of the neck. This might be due to friction from clothing collars, jewelry, and other clothing or accessories. The neck is also a common site for sweat, which could block hair follicles in this area.

It has been revealed that if skin folds at the waist, or clothing waistbands (especially tight ones!) cause friction, it can lead to HS in the waistband area. As a result, HS lesions may show up on the abdomen, back, or sides.

It has been revealed that HS tends to appear on some of the body’s most sensitive places, including the underarms, breasts, groin, and buttocks. These areas are prone to sweat, friction, and irritation from hair removal — all of which may contribute to an HS flare.

If you suspect you have HS, talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can give you a proper diagnosis and help you develop the right treatment and self-care blueprint to combat irritation and flares so you can feel more comfortable in your skin.

HTA Design unveils "UK's largest council housing development"

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (656 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.
  • Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.
  • Construction organization Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Kilian O’Sullivan.

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest new-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction organization Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design said the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

According to recent reports, “Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”.

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” said Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”.

Elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he said.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”.

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley stated the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The new development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he said.

“We recently confirmed that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s fresh Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”.

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) declared the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

Latest Update: 7 Tips for Building a Healthy Diet With Canned, Frozen, and Packaged Goods

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch.
  • Industry observers note that but this suggestion is hardly fair.
  • Sources indicate that besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch. Oftentimes, their videos carry an implicit sense of moral superiority, suggesting that you’re not a good parent (or at least not as good as them) if you’re resorting to pre-packaged store-bought items. Those who pick their own produce and painstakingly hand-craft their own candy necklaces simply work harder, love their children more, are fundamentally better.

Industry observers note that but this suggestion is hardly fair. For the vast majority of people—meaning those who don’t make their living off of wellness content or have near-endless amounts of time and money to burn—canned, frozen, and packaged stuff is almost always a far more practical option. “Groceries are a fortune,” after all, Anthea Levi, MS, RD, a Brooklyn-based health writer and the founder of Alive+Well Nutrition, tells SELF—and fresh items tend to be the most expensive, as a trip to the produce section of the supermarket will readily prove.

Sources indicate that besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power. “You can keep them in your freezer for months, so that often gives people confidence” in the purchase, since they know they don’t have an expiration date hanging over their head, Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. This, in turn, leads to reduced food waste: “Fresh salad greens are notorious for going slimy in the fridge, but you’ll never have that issue with frozen spinach. Ditto for fish. Fresh fish needs to be cooked ASAP before it turns, while frozen fish and canned or tinned fish last until you’re ready to use them,” Levi says.

Nielsen also takes glitch with the basic idea that these options are somehow inherently inferior—“a big, big misconception,” in her eyes. “There has been a lot of confusion about the nature of these foods in general. Just because something is processed or packaged does not mean it’s unhealthy,” she says.

It has been revealed that in other words, canned, frozen, or packaged items are often perfectly fine to include in your diet—and you shouldn’t feel embarrassed, ashamed, or inadequate if they make frequent appearances in your meals (or if they’re your first resort over fresh). “Constant access to fresh foods is, unfortunately, a luxury. If canned, frozen, or packaged items are the only way you’re able to put a fruit or vegetable on your plate, go for it,” Levi indicates. But if you’re still concerned about the health aspect, there are a few key ways to maximize the nutritional value and improve the overall experience. Here’s what to know to make the most of your freezer stash.

“Typically, the fewer ingredients, the better,” Levi says—a rule of thumb to consider while shopping. While canned, frozen, and packaged items have a reputation for being ultra-processed—rife with additives and lower in nutritional value—there are actually plenty out there “that are made from just one or two whole-food ingredients, such as canned peas, frozen fruit, and canned salmon,” Levi says. “These are as close to fresh foods as you can get, and just as nutritious.” Many jarred peanut butters only contain dry roasted peanuts and salt, for example. (By contrast, Ritz peanut butter crackers, which have an ingredients list several rows long, are a very different story.).

According to recent reports, that said, this issue can be nuanced. “Just because an ingredient looks fancy or technical or like a chemical does not necessarily mean that it's bad for you,” Nielsen points out. Many processed foods—including bread, milk, and breakfast cereal—are fortified with healthy vitamins and minerals that you might not otherwise consume enough of in your diet. Take vitamin C—which may appear under the name “ascorbic acid”—as an example. “You might not recognize that what you’re looking at is vitamin C, so you don't want to scare yourself off of potentially nutritious and valuable food because you see things on the ingredients label that you don't recognize,” Nielsen says.

Recent findings suggest that in Nielsen’s experience, canned foods are often considered even less “healthy” than frozen, but the stigma isn’t necessarily warranted. Canned beans, which boast fiber, plant-based protein, and minerals like iron and zinc, are an excellent example of a canned food that amounts to an “incredible nutrition source,” she states. Still, this category does have one major drawback: Staples like veggies, soups, and, yes, beans can contain a significant amount of sodium, a mineral that can cause high blood pressure and related concerns like heart disease and stroke when overconsumed. Tinned fish like TikTok’s beloved sardines can suffer from the same glitch, as the brine inside the tin can be heavy on added salt as well.

Recent findings suggest that given that many brands offer sodium-sensitive alternatives, try to prioritize those options instead to keep your sodium intake in check and avoid potential health consequences, according to Nielsen. Look for labels like “No salt added,” “Low sodium,” or even “No sodium” to steer you in the right direction. If you can’t find anything fitting that bill at your local store, draining and rinsing canned products before use can also drastically cut down on the sodium content—by up to 40%, according to some estimates. (Just keep in mind this method may also cause losses in other nutrients, like vitamin C.).

Recent findings suggest that “In terms of packaged and processed foods, I'm always looking for a couple of nutrients to minimize and a couple of nutrients to optimize,” Nielsen indicates. Sodium is one to limit or avoid, as we’ve already covered, but there are others too—like added sugars and saturated fat. “Peaches that come canned in sugary syrup aren’t as nutritious as peaches that come canned in water, or are purchased frozen or fresh,” for example, Levi says.

In a recent development, on the other hand, when you’re reading over a nutrition facts label, “what you want to see is fiber,” Nielsen says—and “protein is a substantial bonus.” Multiple vitamins and minerals in a product is also often a positive sign. Even breakfast cereals, which are often thought of as unhealthy, “can be incredible sources of minerals like iron and zinc—things that we need that help to keep our metabolism running, that keep us energized,” Nielsen says.

Trying to decide between two (or more) similar products? Comparing and contrasting the ingredients can help you narrow it down, according to Nielsen. Take breakfast cereal: You’ll want to ask yourself, “‘Which one of these cereals gives me the most fiber, the most protein, has the least sugar?’” she says. In this case, the relative content of vitamins and minerals can also be a helpful clue. Seeing that a cereal contains 10% to 20% of your recommended dietary allowance, as many do, can be “your sort of gut check that this is actually a really nutritious food,” Nielsen says.

Industry observers note that even though frozen veggies are affordable and durable, they do have one big downside compared to fresh: Their taste and texture can take a hit—and, in turn, “you do have to adjust your cooking somewhat,” Nielsen notes. To prevent sogginess, cook frozen veggies from frozen rather than letting them defrost first, according to Levi. And you’ll want to use heat-based cooking methods (like air-frying, baking, roasting, and stir-frying) “as opposed to water-based methods like boiling or steaming,” she says.

In a recent development, “Many of us are working more than ever before—maybe working two or three jobs—and we don't have a lot of time to put a home-cooked meal on the table,” Nielsen says. Strategically pairing your canned, frozen, and packaged items is an easy way to boost efficiency in the kitchen without sacrificing nutritional value. If you’re having canned soup for dinner, you can dump in a can of lentils to boost the fiber and protein, for example. (Bonus tip: You can also use this approach to stretch out your leftovers. Need a batch of spaghetti to last longer? Toss some frozen peas on top or some frozen broccoli on the side.).

Sources indicate that “Stocking your freezer and pantry with budget-friendly canned, frozen, and packaged items can help make balanced meals a breeze,” Levi notes. Follow the tried-and-true “plate method” to guarantee a nutritious result, according to Nielsen: Reserve a quarter of your plate for whole grains or starchy vegetables, another quarter for protein, and the remaining half for fruits and non-starchy veggies. You could make rolled oats with chia seeds, frozen berries, and peanut butter for breakfast, or pasta with tinned sardines and frozen broccoli for dinner, for example, Levi says. “It sounds way too simple, but it is backed by so much science to help you balance your diet without counting anything,” Nielsen says. “As long as you stick to that plate method, you will be eating a nourishing diet”—yes, even if your ingredients don’t come to you direct.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following a European tender procedure, the Municipality of Zutphen, Netherlands, has appointed Mecanoo to transform the existing Theatre Hanzehof & Buitensociëteit into a cultural destination. The project, called Hanzehuis, was developed in collaboration with Hanzehof theater, de Muzehof center for the arts, and BIJ de Bieb library, and with ABT Consulting engineers and building services consultant Nelissen. It involves designing a newly introduced center for culture, knowledge and exchange, preserving the main historic building and introducing a new volume to accommodate cultural activities, education and community life under a single roof. Mecanoo contributed to the preparatory phase, and this appointment marks the transition to developing the design further with the professional team, the Municipality and the participating cultural organizations.

It involves designing a latest center for culture, knowledge and exchange, preserving the main historic building and introducing a new volume to accommodate cultural activities, education and community life under a single roof. Mecanoo contributed to the preparatory phase, and this appointment marks the transition to developing the design further with the professional team, the Municipality and the participating cultural organizations.

In a recent development, the Theatre Hanzehof & Buitensociëteit in Zutphen was designed by architect D. Lijsen in 1891. The building was a private social club and concert hall on the edge of the historic Hanseatic city center, noted for its coffered neoclassical ceiling and good acoustics. Since then, it has been renovated and expanded on numerous occasions, including repairs of bomb damage and expansions to modernize the theater. It served as a congress center, theater hall and cinema until 2020, when it was decided to refocus it as a cultural platform. Centrally located within a park-like landscape, the current premises offer the local public a modern theater hall of 550 seats and a concert hall of 600 seats, which host 120 professional concerts and performances per year as well as events by regional groups and social organizations, reaching approximately 75,000 visitors annually.

It has been revealed that mecanoo's Hanzehuis proposal aims to respect the site while introducing a newly introduced volume to accommodate both traditional and new programming. Across the preserved main theater hall, the historic Buitensociëteit and a new timber volume, the cultural center will bring together a theater hall, music and dance studios, a café and flexible spaces for study, work, learning and leisure. According to Mecanoo, the ensemble was conceived as "a living room for the city" rather than "a collection of venues." The different program areas are connected by an interior route called De Straat (The Street), which links the historic structures, the new building and the surrounding park. This circulation space is conceived as an area for informal encounters between visitors, performers, students and the wider community, designed to be transparent, open and accessible. The flexible program supports a broad range of activities, from children's theater and pop concerts to workshops, educational programs and spontaneous gatherings. The center is envisioned as a place where Zutphen's heritage and contemporary cultural life come together.

Estudio A-G uses colour to upgrade 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.
  • Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

Industry observers note that monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely new, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”.

Completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing upcoming energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he said.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”.

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez said, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

Industry observers note that the studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its upcoming owners live today,” he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and newly introduced materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez said, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”.

Industry observers note that he also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.

#103312. How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

📅 19 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1565 w)
